prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, in which neutral atoms trapped at a magic wavelength allow many atoms to be interrogated with the light shift cancelled, bringing optical frequency standards to the 1e-18 level

statement.case_for: I have moved my preferred configuration from B033 (DMFT) to B042, optical lattice clocks, credited to Hidetoshi Katori and Jun Ye. My round-1 reasons for holding back were the overlap with the 2005 and 2012 prizes and the fact that the redefinition of the second has not happened. The exchange has largely settled both for me. Kroll, Pearce and Olsson separate the invention from the toolbox. The comb supplied a ruler for optical frequencies and ion control demonstrated single-system manipulation, whereas the lattice clock's own step is trapping many neutral atoms at the magic wavelength so that the light shift cancels. That step gives a stability and a systematic-uncertainty regime that neither earlier prize covers. The result is original, measured rather than promised, and reproduced in independent laboratories and across fibre links, and the two-name credit has a clear division between the concept and first demonstration (Katori) and the record accuracy (Ye). As a theorist I also note that it is the case where the experiment can be checked against a precise claim without a model-dependent interpretation, which is the property I valued in DMFT and could not fully claim for it. The citation should name the lattice scheme and its realisation at the 1e-18 level and should not mention frequency metrology in general.
statement.case_against: Overlap is not fully dissolved. Mehlig is right that Ye's accuracy work leans on comb and ultrastable-laser technology honoured in 2005, so the novelty rests more on Katori's concept and on accuracy engineering than the two-name symmetry suggests. Danielsson and Pearce concede that Lemonde, Lisdat, Ludlow, Takamoto and others are outside the credit, and nobody on the committee has checked the early-proposal record. I accept the argument that waiting for a CGPM decision is not required, since the prize rewards the demonstrated science, but part of the practical impact is still prospective. Finally this is outside my own field, so I am relying on the atomic-physics members for the technical detail and I discount my own judgment on that point.

responses.point: Olsson argued that the missing credit for Metzner makes B033 hard to defend as a clean configuration in this round, and asked whether a DMFT citation could be framed around the concept and the impurity mapping within the three credited names.
responses.response: I cannot make that framing work. The infinite-dimension limit was the first step and it came from Metzner and Vollhardt, while Georges and Kotliar supplied the impurity mapping and self-consistency. Any citation written around only the mapping would understate the foundation, and one written around the limit would not describe what Georges and Kotliar did. My own round-1 attribution caveat was therefore decisive, as you said, and I withdraw B033 as my preferred prize. It stays as my first alternative because I still think the framework is the most consequential theory advance on the list, but I would not defend it as a discovery with a clean three-name credit.

responses.point: Kroll was asked by the chair whether the stability gained from interrogating many atoms simultaneously is the decisive point of separation of the lattice clock from the 2005 and 2012 prizes, and argued the boundary can be drawn cleanly around the magic-wavelength scheme.
responses.response: I find that persuasive and it is the main reason I moved. Interrogating many atoms at once with the light shift engineered away changes the statistical limit of the clock, which neither a comb nor a single trapped ion offers. I would ask that the citation say this explicitly, so that the many-atom trapping is the thing being honoured. In round 1 I treated B042 as safe to postpone; I no longer see a reason to delay, since the physics is already confirmed by independent groups and is not waiting on a policy step.

responses.point: Mehlig prefers B019 but names B042 as his fallback, noting that Ye's record accuracy leans on frequency-comb technology already honoured in 2005 and that waiting a few years on B019 is not costless.
responses.response: I accept your qualification about Ye and it sharpens the citation: the novelty is the lattice scheme and the accuracy it delivers, not the comb. On B019 I still hold the maturity concern I raised, namely that the pairing mechanism is open and results depend on twist-angle disorder and sample quality, while the first-author experimentalists are outside the three names. I agree with you that a mechanism need not be settled for a discovery to count, as with superconductivity, so I keep B019 as my second alternative and would not oppose it in a few years. Since you accept B042 as a fallback, I see no reason to hold it back for a case that is still evolving.

responses.point: Pearce, as chair, answered my round-1 objection by arguing that the 2005 and 2012 prizes honoured an enabling toolbox, not the lattice invention, and that the prize rewards the demonstration and not a decision by the CGPM.
responses.response: You are right on both points and I have changed my position accordingly. My novelty objection conflated the toolbox with the invention, and my timing objection treated a metrological convention as if it were a scientific test. I also take your point about my own B033: a method whose foundational credit falls partly outside the trio and whose first-principles claims depend on double counting and interaction parameters is a weaker candidate than a measured result with a two-name credit. The priority record for Lemonde, Lisdat, Ludlow and Takamoto is still not checked, and I would ask that the chair have it verified before the ballot.

responses.point: Danielsson argued that overlap with a prize for a tool differs from overlap with the discovery, but conceded that my point about other contributors is real and unresolved and that the two-name attribution is not airtight.
responses.response: I agree that the two-name attribution is not airtight, and I would rather say so than treat it as a closed question. On B057, I continue to regard the physics as overdue and beyond doubt, and my round-1 objection was to the credit, not to the discovery. Your own statement that the trio represents leadership and not discovery-day analysis is why I do not rank it above B042. If the committee adopts a convention for crediting large collaborations, I would revisit it, but I do not think that policy question should be settled in this round at the expense of a cleaner configuration.

uncertainties: Early-proposal and first-demonstration priority for Katori against Lemonde, Lisdat, Ludlow, Takamoto and others, which no member has verified.

Whether the committee accepts that the lattice clock is a distinct invention and not an application of the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control work, given that Ye's accuracy work uses comb and ultrastable-laser technology.
Whether the B042 citation can be worded narrowly enough around the magic-wavelength scheme and many-atom interrogation to keep the 2005 territory visibly outside it.
Whether a DMFT prize could ever be given a clean three-name credit once Metzner is considered, and whether the committee wants to honour a method as a discovery.
statement.conflict_note: I have no recorded personal or institutional tie to Katori, Ye or their groups. My research field (electronic-structure theory, DFT, DMFT-adjacent methods and atomistic spin dynamics) is close to B033 and, less so, to B019, which are now my alternatives rather than my preferred prize; I discount my own enthusiasm for them. B042 is outside my field and I rely on Kroll, Lindroth and Pearce for the technical detail.
